title: Microsoft’s Agent 365 tackles multicloud AI governance
summary: For more than 20 years, I have watched cloud computing evolve from a relatively simple extension of enterprise infrastructure into a distributed collection of platforms, services, data stores, applications, and now AI agents. One lesson has remained clear: Enterprises don’t operate in the clean, single-vendor environments that providers portray in their marketing. They operate in heterogeneous environments. They always have. A company that has standardized on one public cloud for core infrastructure might use another for a specialized data platform, rely on Salesforce for customer engagement, run analytics in Databricks or Snowflake, and deploy dozens of software-as-a-service applications throughout the business. Add the current explosion of AI models, agent platforms, developer tools, and local AI clients, and the need for unified management becomes much more urgent. This is what makes Microsoft’s Agent 365 announcement so significant. Microsoft is positioning Agent 365 as a common control plane for managing, governing, securing, and measuring the value of AI agents across both Microsoft and non-Microsoft platforms. It’s more than another cost dashboard; it acknowledges that multicloud is now the standard operating model for most enterprises. It’s also a refreshingly practical position from a company that has historically built some of the industry’s most successful proprietary technology ecosystems. Enterprises are heterogeneous The biggest disconnect in cloud computing has often been between what providers want customers to do and what customers actually need to do. Providers prefer that enterprises consolidate around their platforms. It makes commercial sense. A larger footprint means more consumption, stronger customer retention, and a better opportunity to sell adjacent services. However, enterprise architecture doesn’t work that way.
